full_judgment:
6. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka having considered the evidence and the relevant materials on record, found the appellants guilty under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code and sentenced each of them to suffer imprisonment for life and also to pay a fine of taka 20,000.00 each, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for further 6[six] months. 

 9. Mr. Md. Shakhawat Hossain Khan, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellants, submits that the trial Court and the High. Court Division erred in law and fact in convicting them and maintaining the same. He further submits that both the judgments and orders of conviction and sentence are illegal and not based on any legal evidence. He further submits that the FIR lodged in the case by Pw-1 in pursuant to G.D. Entry No.823 dated 17.05.1995 being the result of investigation is inadmissible in evidence. He further submits that the evidence adduced by Pw-1 is based on hearsay statement. The staffs of the hotel referred in the FIR were all arrested in the case and forwarded to the Magistrate as accused and their statements were recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Magistrate who recorded their statements was not examined in the trial and could not be subjected to any cross- examination and the learned trial Court illegally End improperly relied upon confessional statements of arrested accused. Subsequently, Pws'-4 and 5 and put reliance on their statements illegally and improperly. He further submits that none of the five witnesses identified the appellants in the Court during trial and for this non-recognition of the appellants by any witness, a strong doubt arises about their complicity in the alleged occurrence. He further submits that the prosecution case became shaky and the defence also lost the chance to establish important circumstances and materials in their favour. It is also submitted that in the FIR lodged on 17.05.1995 at 07:50 a.m it is disclosed that Pw-4, Subhas Das initially stated before Pty-1, Sub-Inspector of Police that he did not know about the identity of the deceased and did not have knowledge about commission of the occurrence of murder. It is submitted that the investigating officer, the Magistrate who recorded the statement of the witnesses, any hotel staff, any inmate of the hotel, any neighbourers were not examined during trial. Even no sketch map was prepared about the place of occurrence and no alamats were produced in Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court did-not consider the evidence of Pw-4, Hotel Manager, that on the night of occurrence, the accused's name were not in the register of the hotel. He further submits that both the Courts below did not consider that Pw-3, Nazrul, alone came with ocular evidence about the appellants' alleged involvement, but he was not corroborated by any witness of the hotel. He further submits that there was no legal evidence whatsoever in the case and the findings of the learned trial Court are heavily based on suppression of facts and hearsy evidence. He further submits that both Pw's4 and 5 did not come forward in the trial Court with any specific case of identification of any of the appellants. 

 10. On the other hand, Mr. Sujit Chattarje, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing on behalf, of the respondent State, contends that the prosecution successfully proved the place of occurrence, time and date of occurrence by the consistent evidence. He adds that though Pw-5 was declared hostile in respect of his identification of the accused in the dock, his evidence would not be discarded inasmuch as he corroborated the other incriminating materials in respect of murder of the deceased. He also contends that the evidence of Pw-5 was well corroborated by Pw-3 in respect of injuries and other incriminating materials by Pw-4. Therefore; the conviction and sentence imposed upon them based on evidence on record calls for no interference by this Division. 

 12. Prior to looking into the merits of the sentence, let us examine the evidence of Pws first as to how and why and who committed the occurrence of killing the victim Yeachilong Karucha Alexander Yeah [deceased]. 

 25. Upon perusal of the entire evidence on record along with the judgment of the trial court as well as the Appellate Court, it appears that the prosecution case mainly rests upon the evidence of Pw-5 who is a guard of that Hotel. Pw-5 is not the eye witness of the commission of the murder but he deposed that on 17.05.1995 at night while he was sleeping, around 12 O'clock another guard Siraj gave him the key of the gate saying that at room no 09, Tokai Khokon and Malu Khokon were staying. At 4 0 clock of that night Tokai Khokon and Malu Khckon called him and asked to open the gate of the hotel which he declined to do. They threatened him at gun point and therefore, he opened the gate. He witnessed that the dead body of the victim was brought down to the road by Tokai Khokon and Malu Khokon. They then inflicted dagger blow upon the knee of the victim. This Pw-5, guard Nazrul, disclosed this incident to the assistant manager, supervisor and another guard Siraj. Pw-4 corroborated the testimony of Pw-5 deposing that hearing the incident he found the dead body of the victim on the road and came to know from guard Nazrul Islam that Tokai Khokon and Malu Khokon murdered the victim. It appears that the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court convicted the accused based mainly on circumstantial evidence since there is no direct evidence of commission of murder by the accused. Bringing down the dead body of the victim to road by Tokai Khokon and Malu Khokon and then inflicting dagger blow upon the knee of the victim by them are the circumstances relevant against the accused. When accused Are held responsible based on circumstantial evidence, court must be cautious about drawing conclusion from the circumstantial evidence. The Court must adopt cautious approach while basing its conviction purely on circumstantial evidence [State of Haryana Vs. Ved Prakash, AIR 1994 SC 468]. Circumstantial evidence should be of such a nature that there should not be any gap in the chain of circumstantial evidence. Jurisprudence that has been built up regarding circumstantial evidence through case laws should be meticulously reviewed before reaching concrete conclusion in the light of the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 "It is a settled principle of law that the prosecution has to satisfy certain conditions before a conviction based on circumstantial evidence can be sustained. The circumstances from which the conclusion of quilt is to be drawn should be fully established and should also be consistent with only one hypothesis, i.e. the guilt of the accused. The circumstances -should be conclusive and proved by the prosecution. There must be a chain of events so complete so as not to leave any substantial doubt in the mind of the Court. Irresistibly, the evidence should lead to the conclusion inconsistent with the innocence of the accused and the only possibility that the accused has committed the crime." 

 "Needless to say that in a case in which the evidence is of a circumstantial nature the facts and circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is said to be drawn by the prosecution must be fully established beyond all reasonable doubt and the facts and the circumstances so established should not only be consistent with the guilt of the appellant but also they must entirely be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and must exclude every reasonable hypothesis consistent with his innocence." 

 28. In the case of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda vs State of Maharashtra [AIR 1984 SC 1622]. (1984) 4 SCC 116 the Court elaborately considered the standard of proof required for recording a conviction on the basis of circumstantial evidence and laid down the golden principles of standard of proof required in a case sought to be established on the basis of circumstantial evidence which are as follows: 

 (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused." 

 29. These five criteria to base a conviction on circumstantial evidence were again discussed in the case of Prakash-Vs-State of Rajasthan FAIR, 2013 SC 1474]. 

 30. It appears from the decisions quoted above that in case of conviction of accused based on circumstantial evidence there must be a chain of events/evidence so complete as not to leave any reason-able ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused. 

 31. Let us consider whether the conviction of the accused mainly on the basis of circumstantial evidence on record is justified or not. In the instant case before lodging FIR with the police station, in pursuance of GD entry no 823 of Sutrapur police station dated 17.05.95, at around 6:35 a.m on 17.05.95, police went to the place where the dead body of the victim was lying on the road for holding inquest. Dead body of the victim was identified by Suvash Chandra Das (PW-4), manager of the hotel Mostari, where the victim had been staying for the last four years before his death. In the inquest report it was categorically stated by the officer holding inquest that locally no one could say anything about the death of the victim. If Pw-5, guard Nazrul, told Suvash Chandra Das (PW-41) on 17.05.95 at 4 a.m about bringing down the dead body of the victim to road by Tokai Khokon and Malu khokon and then inflicting dagger blow upon the knee of the victim by them, he (Suvash Chandra Das) would have informed the officer holding inquest of the dead body of the victim at the same date at 6:35 a.m of that matter, he being the person to identify the dead body of the victim for the purpose of holding inquest. In the instant case officer holding the inquest and the informant of this case being the same person definitely there would have been description in this respect in the first information report which is absent in the present case. It appears that missing of this point in FIR creates a gap in the chain of circumstantial evidence which necessarily creates doubt regarding the prosecution version of the case. In case where the prosecution endeavours to introduce at the trial a new version or a version which is materially different from the original, as narrated in the first information report, Court, as a rule of prudence, is required to act with utmost care and circumspection in scrutinizing the evidence [Nirmal Singh-Vs-State of Himachal Pradesh, 1987 CrLJ 1644] 

 32. In the instant case it is stated in the FIR as well as in the charge framed against the accused that manager of hotel Mostari (Suvash Das) informed that the deceased victim was a boarder of room no 05 of Hotel Mostari but he did not stay in the room at that night. If the deceased victim did not stay in room no 05 at that night, how could his dead body be dragged from room no 5 to the road? Moreover, there is no documentary evidence on record to the effect that accused were the boarders of room No.9 of the hotel Mostari at that night. Pw-4 deposed during cross-examination, "আমি চাইনিজ বোর্ডারের রুমে ঘটনার রাত্রিতে কে আসে বলতে পারিনা। কারা তাকে কিভাবে মারে কখন মারে তা দেখি নাই। বোর্ডার মারা যাওয়ায় আমরা প্রেসারে ছিলাম। মালু খোকন ঘটনার দিন কয়টায় আমাদের হোটেলে আসে বলতে পারিনা। আমি টোকাই খোকন ও মালু খোকন নামে কাউকে চিনিনা।" This portion of the deposition of Pw-4 clearly indicates that 4 does not have any idea about Tokai Khokon and Malu Khokon or as to who paid visit to the Chinese boarder's room on the night of the occurrence. The deposition of Pw-4 during cross- examination by Tokai Khokon that he does not know as to who came to the Chinese boarder's room on the night of the occurrence is contradictory to the deposition of Pw-5 since he deposed that he (Pw-5) informed whose assistant manager (Pw-4) of the occurrence. Pw- 5 deposed, "আমি ঘটনার কথাecution সহকারী ম্যানেজার পরিমল সুপারভাইজার দারোয়ান সিরাজকে বলি।" If Tokai Khokon and Malu Khokon made frequent visits to Hotel Mostari, Pw-4 was supposed to know their identity. Guard Nazrul Islam (Pw-5) is the vital witness in the instant case. He deposed during examination in chief, "ডকের আসামিদের এখন ঠিকমত চিন্তে পারছি না। During cross examination by Tokai Khokon he deposed "টোকাই খোকন ও মালু খোকন নামে দুই লোক ঘটনার রাত্রিতে আমাদের হোটেলে ছিল। কিন্তু আমি ফাদের ভাল মত চিনিনা।" He could not properly identify the accused on the dock. This does not matter since it may be difficult for a witness to recognize an accused after long period of interval from first meeting. But the fact that guard Nazrul fled at the beginning of the incidence coupled with his not being able to properly recognize the accused on the dock has made his conduct suspicious one for which it would not be appropriate to rely solely upon his evidence keeping aside other relevant facts and circumstances having effect upon the merits of the case. 

 33. Magistrate who recorded the statement of guard Siraj, witness Suvash Chandra Das and Nazrul Islam under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Code did not depose before the Court but reliance has been placed upon the statement of guard Siraj during trial which does- not appear to be justified since no explanation has been offered for non-examination of the abovementioned Magistrate. Witness Siraj had not been examined by the prosecution. Guard Siraj appear to be a very material witness in the present case whose evidence could throw light in controversial issues of the case but the prosecution could not produce him without providing any explanation for the same. Though calling a witness is within the discretion of the prosecution, the same has to be exercised fairly. In the case of Mohammed. Kassim-Vs-R. 11956, Malayan 11 212 (Penang HC), Sarkar Law of Evidence by M C Sarkar, S C Sarkar and P C Sarkar, 19th Edition, Volume 2 page 2314] it was held that "Calling of witness is a matter for the discretion of the prosecution and the pr6secution need not call every witness from whom a statement has been taken However, this discretion must be exercised fairly." 

 34. It is the duty of the party to lead the best evidence in its possession which could throw light on the issue in controversy and in case such a material evidence is withheld, the court may draw adverse inference under section 114 illustration (g) of the Evidence Act, 1872 notwithstanding that the onus of proof did not lie on such party and it was not called upon to produce the said evidence [Mussauddin Ahmed Vs-State of Assam, (2009) 14 SCC 541]. 

 35. In the case in hand, motive of the accused to commit the instant murder has not been established. Though prosecution is not bound to prove motive in case of proof of offence by ocular evidence, motive may sometimes be relevant under section 8 of the Evidence Act, 1872 in case of proof of offence by circumstantial evidence. "Motive, though not a sine qua non for bringing the offence home to the accused, is relevant and important on the question of intention. Though the prosecution is not bound to prove motive for the crime, absence of any motive is a factor which may be considered in determining the guilt of the accused. The question of motive is not material where there is direct evidence of the acts of the accused and the acts themselves are sufficient to disclose the intention of the actor. But in cases of circumstantial evidence, absence of motive is a factor in favour of the accused [The Indian Renal Code by Ratanlal and Dhirajlal, 34th Edition, Volume-1, page number ccclxxviii]." In a case whose fate depends mainly on circumstantial evidence motive of the accused to commit the offence charged with is of fundamental importance, although in all other case, such as, where the accused is sought to be connected with the offence by direct evidence, prosecution is not required to prove the motive [THE STATE-Vs-LALU MIAH and ANO. 39 DLR(AD) (1987) 117]. 

 36. Criminal jurisprudence as has been built up requires proof beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt for conviction of an offender. Now, the question arises whether the evidence on record is of such an unimpeachable in nature that the prosecution has been able to prove the case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. What is reasonable doubt is a question of fact and has to be determined in the light of the facts and circumstances of a particular case. Doubt should not emanate from mere vague apprehensions rather it should spontaneously arise from analysis of the evidence on record with-reason and common sense. In the case of Ramakant Rai —vs- Madan Rai and Ors, [AIR 2004 SC 77] it was held that: 

 "Doubts would be called reasonable if they are free from a zest for abstract speculation. Law cannot afford any favourite other than truth. To constitute reasonable doubt, it must be free from an over emotional response. Doubts must be actual and substantial doubts as to the guilt of the accused persons arising from the evidence, or from the lack of it, as opposed to mere vague apprehensions. A reasonable doubt is not an imaginary, trivial or a merely possible doubt; but a fair doubt based upon reason and commonsense. It must grow out evidence in the case." 

 37. In the instant case, the gap in the chain of circumstantial evidence along with the lack of, infirmity and contradiction in evidence essentially gives rise to a doubt about the prosecution case which appears to be reasonable in the facts and circumstances of the case.
